question: What is the main reason we report certain diseases to public health authorities?

options.A: To bill insurance companies for hospital admissions
options.B: To report specific illnesses to public health authorities
options.C: To track daily hospital staff attendance records
options.D: To update patient medical history in private files

explanation: You got this! Disease notification simply means letting health officials know about dangerous illnesses so they can jump in quickly and stop outbreaks before they spread. Great job! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is it so important to report a disease outbreak quickly in your community?

options.A: It guarantees free medical treatment for all citizens
options.B: It stops patients from visiting traditional healers
options.C: It helps health agencies spot unusual disease patterns early
options.D: It reduces the cost of prescription drugs in pharmacies

explanation: Spotting cases early gives health teams the heads-up they need to track trends and stop epidemics in their tracks. You're building solid public health sense! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h1)

question: How can we best describe public health surveillance?

options.A: A method for punishing clinics that lose patient files
options.B: A financial audit of private clinic expenditures
options.C: An ongoing system of collecting and analyzing health data
options.D: A one-time yearly census of hospital bed capacity

explanation: Think of surveillance as a continuous watch, not just a one-off check. We keep gathering and reviewing health data day in and day out to stay ahead of sickness! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h2)

question: During a health emergency, how do health ministries use surveillance data?

options.A: To allocate scarce medical resources where they are needed most
options.B: To select which nursing students receive scholarships
options.C: To decide which private hospitals should be closed permanently
options.D: To determine salary increases for hospital administrators

explanation: Good data shows us exactly where an outbreak is hitting hardest. That way, we can rush medications, supplies, and staff right where they'll save the most lives. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which type of diseases must be reported the absolute fastest because they can spark sudden outbreaks?
explanation: Diseases like cholera or measles move fast! We call these epidemic-prone, and they need immediate reporting so we can protect the community. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h3)

question: A nurse identifies a case of polio. Why do we place polio in a special, urgent reporting category?

options.A: It is a targeted disease for global eradication and elimination
options.B: It only affects elderly patients in urban hospitals
options.C: It is a common seasonal allergy with mild symptoms
options.D: It does not require tracking by government agencies

explanation: The world is actively trying to wipe out polio completely. Because every single case is a global emergency, we track them with extreme urgency! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h3)

question: Who starts the whole disease-reporting chain right at the grassroots level?

options.A: The administrative clerk in charge of billing
options.B: The frontline nurse or doctor who assesses the patient
options.D: The federal minister of health in the capital city

explanation: That's you! The nurse or clinician at the bedside or clinic floor who first sees the patient is always the crucial first link in the reporting chain. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h4)

question: If a nurse at a rural primary health center diagnoses Lassa fever, who must be notified immediately next in the reporting chain?

options.A: The federal ministry of finance budget office
options.C: The Local Government Area surveillance officer
options.D: The World Health Organization headquarters overseas

explanation: Reporting flows step-by-step from the local clinic straight to the Local Government Area (LGA) team before heading to the state and national levels. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h4)

question: What standard framework guides disease reporting forms in Nigerian health facilities?

options.A: Standard Operating Procedures for Pharmacy Inventory
options.B: National Curriculum for Basic Nursing Education

explanation: IDSR is the golden framework we use across Nigerian facilities to keep our disease tracking organized and consistent. You'll see this a lot in practice! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is a common mistake nurses should avoid when suspecting a notifiable disease outbreak?

options.A: Informing the local government health team too quickly
options.B: Using standard case definition sheets during patient assessment
options.C: Waiting for full laboratory confirmation before reporting the suspect case
options.D: Submitting weekly summary logs to public health authorities

explanation: Never wait for lab results if you suspect a dangerous outbreak! Report based on clinical signs right away so health teams can act fast. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the main goal of 'active case finding' during an outbreak?

options.A: To conduct routine training for nursing students
options.B: To audit the financial accounts of the local hospital
options.C: To replace expired medications in the pharmacy store
options.D: To search for additional unrecorded cases in the community

explanation: Instead of waiting for sick people to walk into the clinic, active case finding means going out into the community to find anyone else who might be hiding or missing treatment. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why do public health teams collect blood or stool samples during a suspected outbreak?

options.A: To test the quality of local drinking water pipes only
options.B: To measure the general nutritional status of healthy adults
options.C: To calculate the daily operational costs of the clinic
options.D: To identify the specific causative agent in a laboratory

explanation: Lab tests on these samples tell us the exact germ, bacteria, or virus causing the trouble, helping us choose the exact right treatment. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why are community health nurses usually the first to notice an unusual disease cluster?

options.A: Because they only review paperwork sent from foreign countries
options.B: Because they spend all their time working in national research labs
options.C: Because they focus entirely on hospital financial accounting
options.D: Because they interact daily with families and local groups

explanation: Community nurses are right on the ground! Because you work closely with local families every day, you're in the best position to spot when something feels off. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h7)

question: How can nurses help stop community members from hiding infectious illnesses out of fear?

options.A: Refusing to treat patients who do not speak English
options.B: Keeping all health information secret from local leaders
options.C: Threatening penalties for families that miss immunization days
options.D: Building trust through health education and supportive care

explanation: When we show empathy, educate gently, and create a safe space without judgment, community members feel comfortable coming to us early. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h7)

question: What is a common hurdle that slows down prompt disease reporting in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Excessive availability of advanced laboratory computers
options.B: Too many trained surveillance officers in every clinic
options.C: Zero workload for nurses during morning shifts
options.D: Shortage of reporting forms and poor transport

explanation: Logistical challenges like running out of paper forms or lacking transport to deliver them can unfortunately drag down reporting times. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h8)

question: How can health facilities best fix the problem of staff underreporting due to a fear of blame?

options.A: By firing every nurse who makes a minor documentation error
options.B: By hiding all disease statistics from the government ministry
options.C: By stopping all surveillance activities during busy seasons
options.D: By fostering a supportive, blame-free work culture that values data

explanation: When staff know they won't be unfairly punished for honest mistakes, they are much more open and accurate with their reporting. Spot on! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h8)
